Title: Stories that stick
Author: Kinda hall
Notes:
Good overview of business storytelling and a basic story formula for different use cases. Stories that stick...
Stories are what make us human. We have the ability to create fictions individually and collectively.
Stories have a beginning, middle, and end...1. Normal life2. Explosion3. New normal
Not everything is a story:Stories include...• Identifiable character, or several single characters• Authentic emotion. The emotion felt by the characters or inherent in the story, not the audience. This is how to get empathy• A significant moment. Specific point in time/space/circumstance that sets it apart from the rest of our existence. Moment magnifies a specific piece of a sprawling space. Go small and detailed. Zoom in, be specific. Don't stay high-level or too vague• Specific details. Details and imagery to draw in the audience. Details signal to the audience how deeply the storyteller understands them. Specific details engage the imagination of the audience

Four stories:• Value story. Value to the people who need it. Value gap between product and customer.• Resist the temptation to fill gap with features and information. This is system 2 thinking. Lists, bullets, price comparisons, benefits, features.• Keep people in system 1 thinking. Automatic. Anything you can do to reduce cognitive strain is usually best. Ease, not mental strain• It's so much more than that... (the features)• If you can't talk about your product or show it to anyone, what would you say to customers?• - what's left? The people using it.• Value story• What pain or problem is your customer experiencing, what keeps them up at night? - normal• How does your product make their life better, solve the pain? - explosion• How is life different after, what pain points have vanished, how do they feel? - new normal• Have identifiable character. Have the person you offer services to be the center of your story, not your service. You must include a character to care about.• Authentic emotion. "You have to get into bed with them". What do they worry about before they go to sleep? What keeps them awake? The only emotions that matter are those in your potential customer, or the character in your story• A moment. Often connected to the explosion.• Specific details. You cannot fake thus. You need to know your audience, and some details they can connect with.• Founder Story. Every business has a story.• A founder story helps you stand out.• We tend to use the same differentiators as everyone else, thus we are the same. The solution is the founder story.• When all of the offers look the same, we go with the one where we love the story.• It's not the magnitude of the story, it's the decision to tell it• This story bridges the gap between the company and investors, building a team (securing talent), and getting customers• If you have started a business, you have a founder story• Where does it hide?• Go way back... moments in your young self• When you said "There has to be a better way..."• Look for the "blood, sweat, and tears"• Pitfalls• Founder story is not the value story• Not telling founder story because you are tired of telling it• This story isn't for you, it's for them.• Thinking you can't tell it, because you are not the founder.• Transition into the story. "I remember the day I heard the story, I was doing such and such, etc. The story as I heard it..."• "I knew..., and I hope you feel that too"• Letting reluctant founder shutdown the founder story.• If you tell the story right, authentically, it is not self-agrandizing• Stories sound like life• Identifiable characters: centered on founder• Authentic emotion: consider what audience cares about. Investors care you can handle frustration and doubt, and that you have determination and commitment, pride, etc. Customers care about what drove you to create the product.• A moment: include a big moment/explosion. A date, the weather, a day.• Specific details: audience specific. Path navigating• ... one of the easiest stories to forget to tell is the founder story.• Most of the time, you don't get a second chance to tell your story• Purpose story.• Purpose over profit. People are motivated by transcendent purpose.• We are wired to attribute meaning and purpose. If you don't do it, people will it it for you.• People use stories to align around goals or purposes. Uniting, clarifying, motivating.• Must be nonhypocritical• How strongly the story supports a specific message. What point do I want to make? What do I want my audience to think, feel, do?• Little room for error. Main character of a purpose story is typically the leader telling the story. If you tell it wrong, you will have told the story for the story's sake, becoming seen as an "arrogant" leader.• How to match: have a clear message. Then think, when have I learned this message? When have I seen this?• The best purpose stories are your own stories. Share the emotions you felt about the event. Vulnerability. Being vulnerability in business is the heartbeat of innovation, etc.• Running a successful business is vulnerability.• Purpose story often coincides with the explosion. Zoom in and share this part in slow motion.• Make the your own story feel likenit is about your audience, with specific details they can relate to.• Employees should know about their company history and story? "Family history". Brings meaning, purpose, and belonging.• Intentional storytelling is what builds and sustains culture. The same as it is for families telling their origin stories.• Do they know they are part of something bigger?• Customer Story. • Brand is what people say about you behind your back, when you're not listening• The customers tell the customer story. Not the company• The customer story thus has inherent credibility.• Ask for these stories.• Guide the response by asking the right questions.• What did you use before, have you noticed anything different after using it? Elicits a story with normal, explosion, new normal• Tell stories where there is a void in attention, when people have room for hearing a story.• Customer story is about customer. How to show them as relatable? Perfection is your enemy, there needs to be imperfect details to be realistic and believable, don't remove imperfection• Emotion from the normal, before the product. The new normal only matters in contrast to the old normal emotions.

Do I have a story? Everyone has a storyStory collecting:• Our stories attach to the nouns in our life.• People• Places• Things• Events• Think about firsts• First time you tried...• First date...• First...• May not be the story you choose, but will unlock more memories• Make list of customer objections and questions• Look for stories that resolve these concerns• Ask yourself lots of questions• When have you had to be resourceful to survive• What was the worst day in history of business• When have you made a customer cry for good or bad reason• When have you stopped a customer from crying• What's the hardest thing you have ever done in business• Who's life is different because of your business• What is your proudest moment in your work or business• What one event or decision in your history could your company not have survived without• When have you been surprised or mistaken about someone or something• What was your first or most meaningful sale• When have you lost a sale• Who is your most satisfied or least satisfied customer• When was your most embarrassing moment• When has someone said you couldn't accomplish something• What was the moment you knew your work is worth itStory choosing:• The right story vs any story• Pick from the four stories• Value story if you want more effective sales and marketing• Founder story if you want to increase competence and differentiate• Purpose story if you want to align and engage team• Customer story if you want better sales, marketing, and credibility• Which objective is most pressing?• About telling the story.• The audience• Who are you telling to?• What do you want them to think, feel, or do?
Finding stories in the moment:• Jot things down. Record what you see, the stories around you
..........Crafting your story:Ideas come and go. Stories stay
Explosions are usually where our stories start. This is when we notice the story.Start with the explosion and then work backward.
Normal: most fun and most important.Flex empathetic muscles. Help them settle in and let down their guard.Include details about character, emotion, particular moment, and familiar details for audience. This is a simple checklist to walk through
New normal:Use it as an opportunity to circle back to normal, but with the new information, product, benefit, etc.

Well played stories don't need gimmicks or tactics.
A story should be as long as it needs to be. Can be 10 seconds, or 90 mins.Start with the full-blown long story, write it all out. Then cut back on content and condense.Don't get rid of the most important parts for the sake of brevity.
Make your pitch a story, not a pitch. Elevator pitch is a story.

Craft the story for the goal of the story.You likely have the right story, but haven't crafted it well to suit your goal
.............
Any moment can become a story.
Stories change moments.They change context, they change minds, they create connectionTell your stories

Telling your story.Tips:• Start with a story. Easy way to ease tension between audience and speaker• Be careful about images you use in slides. Let the audience create images from relevant context in their lives. They create it for themselves and thus find your story more relatable.• Only use nondescript images.• Don't rely on photos to tell your story.• Practice can break perfect. If you are too flawless, it doesn't work. A balance between being well prepared and over rehearsed. Let go of perfect, and it will let go of you.• Focus on the message• Tell the story that feels right to you. Only tell the stories you are comfortable telling. If you are not ready to tell it, or it doesn't feel right, don't tell it.• You don't have to overshare. There is likely another story to get the message across• When you have a real story to tell, it's natural. Storytelling is natural. Get out of your own way. If a story resonates with you, it will almost tell itself.
We want to hear stories, because we are human. Tell stories. Storytellers have influence.
Our lives are all story.
.....................

Ellicit Oxytocin through story telling, empathy
On the other end of your data is a person.
A brand is not a story

Title: The happiness trap
Author: Russ harris
Notes: We are naturally mindful in many situations that are novel or exciting (a date with someone we love, a beautiful view in nature). We get bored because we are not mindful, we are hooked by or fused with feelings or judgements that what is happening is bad or subpar in some way. Learning to experience life with more mindfulness and unhook from subjective judgements about our reality in each moment can help us see life for the beauty that it is. We get tired of things because we start to feel that we know them and there is nothing to pay attention to (we know the story the protocol, we know what will happen, we don’t need to notice anymore). Contrary to this assumption, things are always changing in our life, and we simply don’t notice. Savor every moment. One could say that to truly live as if you only live once means that you not only seek out pleasure, but enjoy the mundane and even attention to and notice the pain and discomfort because you won’t get it ever again. Discomfort often points to something important: something you need to do, something you care about, etc. We ruminate worry and obsess because it gives us temporary rewards. For example, escape, feeling like we are working hard, avoiding taking action. These payoffs or rewards are called reinforcing consequences. Our internal world is like a documentary. It misses 99% of what we have done in our life, and is often biased, yet it paints a specific picture and insists that this is who we are. It is The Big Story or our self-concept. Choose goals that are live person goals, not dead person goals, things that a live person can do better than a dead person. Instead of saying “i’ll stop smoking”, say “instead of smoking, i’ll run around the block, etc. Focus on what will replace what you want to change. Focus on starting things that make life better, a values-based life, rather than stopping things, a rules-based life. You will accomplish the rules along the way, or find out they were flawed anyway. Values are like what we bring to life’s table. We can’t choose what dishes are served, they change all the time, some are enjoyable for us, some are not. We can choose, though, to bring something to the table. Values can guide us in what we bring. Values are ways that we live in the present, the way we act toward the world, the way we become. Goals  are things to obtain. Goals are not mindful practices, they are the ends of practices that may be mindful or not. Our poor behavior doesn’t reflect our values, it means we are hooked by thoughts and feelings that pull us away from our values.  Values are desired qualities of behavior, how we want to behave, because we can choose. If there is something you aspire to be, by definition, that way of being is already a value you have. The only way to know if it’s really yours, if you really like it, if it’s really a benefit to you, is by trying it out, by tasting the food. You can smell and think all you want, philosophize all you want, but the knowing only comes by doing/trying. Take one bite, think small, take baby steps. Small steps over time have large effects. Choose a value or two each morning that you will bring into play that day.  As you try it, notice what it is like, see what you feel and think about it, if it’s doing what you want for you. Make small changes in one area of your life, like a sculptor. You can’t focus on them all at the same time. You have to chip in one spot and try to make that what you want before moving to another spot. You always have two choices for making things better: leave the situation, or stick with it and do what you can to influence it for the better and ask for help and treat yourself kindly. You can’t always leave, but you can always do your part to make something better.  Domains of life: work, relationships, play/recreation, health. All domains overlap. So small changes in one create a domino effect. You can ripple positive change into your life. Find values in each domain. Some may appear in multiple domains. Now that you have domains and values, pick one domain for the week, and one short-term goal based on those values, that is not too easy or hard, not not emotional or based on how to feel, and not a dead person goals. Make it specific, realistic, and anticipate that it will be hard. We always can choose our attitude, our way in life. We only have the present. The past is memory in the present, the future images and thought in the present, but the present is experience. Savor it and make the most of it.

Title: It didn’t start with you
Author: Mark wolynn
Notes: Keeping silent about the past does little to help future generations. Trauma in families can be experienced down to the 3rd or 4th generation, much like reactions to a scent in future generations of rats. This occurs perhaps through gene activation/deactivation. We find this trauma by discovering a core sentence about our trauma and matching it to the first ancestor to experience these things. Are you sure this fear originates with you? This book is a case against keeping quiet about your history. We think we are more likely to propagate bad behavior by talking about it, but we also run the risk of not naming it and our kids unknowingly following in our footsteps. By avoiding the topics and our past, we are more likely to find our children reliving our pains, both they and us in oblivion. Ignoring the pain deepens it. This book is also another book that could have been much shorter than it was. Interesting information and helpful tools for people, but a bit of a drag for someone trying to get to the pit and core of the ideas as clearly and quickly as possible. We use our pain, only by naming it and leaving it in our own past, not hiding it in the lives of future generations. We choose partners that will best help us finish Unfinished business with our parents, selves, family history, etc. Lay down nee pathways in your brain, leaving pains of the past with those in the past. See with compassion all around you in the present and past.

Title: Ultralearning
Author: Scott H Young
Notes:
Metalearning - draw a map:
Meta = beyondLearning about learningHow is knowledge structured or organized in this language
Ultralearning projects can be done faster than traditional one-size-fits-all education format.
Short-term research strategies:Why: motivation for learningWhat: knowledge and abilities you will need to acquire to be successfulHow: resources, environment, and methods you will use
Why?Instrumental: as a means to another outcome. In this case, do additional research to see if this will actually help you achieve your goalintrinsic: for its own sake
What?Concepts: anything that needs to be understood. Math, etc.Facts: need to be memorized. Don't need to understand too deeply, just recall at timesProcedures: anything that needs to be practiced, may not involve much conscious thinking at all. Riding a bike, etc. Pronunciation
Underline potential bottlenecks
How?Benchmarking: find common ways people learn this subjectEmphasize-exclude method: first find areas of study that align with goals you identified. Omit or delay elements of benchmark curriculum that don't align with your goals.

How much planning should you do?Most people fail to do enough. Some people use it to procrastinate though. Just get started.Use about 10% of your learning time to researchReassessing your research regularly is important.
Law of diminishing returns: the more time you invest in an activity, the weaker and weaker the benefits will be as you get closer to your results.If your research time benefited you more than your learning time, your research is likely helpful.If your learning time benefited you more than your research time, your research is likely NOT helpful.
Longterm:Each project will improve your general metalearning skills. Longterm metalearning is something you acquire through experience. You have to out in the work, there is no one-size-fits-all approach.

....................
Focus - sharpen your knife:
An exceptional ability for focus. An ability to focus quickly and easily
3 Struggles with focus:
Starting (procrastinating). Why do we procrastinate? There is an aversion for this activity, or a craving for something else.Recognize when you are procrastinating. Acknowledge it. Are you more averse, or simply more interested in something else?Most of what is unpleasant in a task is an impulse that doesn't exist after the first few minutes. Take 5 or 10 minutes and just start.Try the pomodoro technique if 5 minutes doesn't help.I can only quit right after I have done something successful.Go back to the start to your ignored tasks and practice the pomodoro technique.You must be conscious in your time decisions.You cannot control your impulses, but you can learn to respond better
Sustaining (getting distracted). When you fail to stay focused.Flow, is often used as the model of focus to sustain. Flow is inconsistent with demand for deliberate practice. A flow state is not impossible in ultralearning, but it is unlikely.Resistance to what is natural is part of difficult learning. Don't worry about flow or seek it. Push through frustrating sessions. Your deliberate practice now will make later sessions more enjoyable.People remember more when practice is broken in different studying periods, and interleaved topics. Study various aspects/skills of a subject during your study session. Cover a few topics rather than one. 15 mins - 1 hour is generally fine for a subject.Sources of distraction:Environment.Task. Some activities are more difficult than others.Your mind. Random thoughts, restlessness, daydreaming, emotional wounds. Acknowledge the feeling, and gently go back to task. This will become easier and easier over time as you practice.
Optimizing quality (the right kind of focus).Two variables:Arousal: overall level of energy or alertness. Too much or too little is not helpful.High arousal: narrow, brittle focus. Athletics.Low/relaxed arousal: math, creativity. Wide focus. Eureka moments. Taking a break can encourage this by allowing mind to broaden view.
Improving focus:Try sitting still for longer than you have before. Practice not reacting to distractions, responding by refocusing................
Directness - go straight ahead:He who can go to the fountain does not go to the water jar
Directly learning the thing we want seems too uncomfortable, boring, or frustrating. So we settle for some book, lecture, or app.
Directness = kind of like Transfer Appropriate Processing in psych literature.
Learning done with connection the context in which the skills learned will eventually be used.
Many self-directed learners fall into the trap of indirect learning. Duolingo is an example.Most students use listening to a lecture as the main way they learn material.You must do the thing you want to get good at. Spend a lot of time doing the thing. Do the thing and you shall have the power.
Sometimes the exact situation is not available for you to practice in.


Transfer: education's dirty secret.It has largely failed to occur. Learning something in one setting, and applying it in another.It's an education scandal.
A student who has studied examples, often cannot solve problems that deviate from the examples.
Transfer does exist, yet it is paradoxical. When we want it, it doesn't happen. But we do it all the time. Comparison is transfer. The more knowledge we get, it becomes easier to transfer.Most formal learning is indirect.Far transfer is reduced with greater direct learning.Directness also helps in that real situations share details with other real situations, as opposed to theoretical situations.
Learning subjects often sticks stubbornly to the situations they are learned in.
When learning new things, tie them as closely as possible to the situations you will use it in.
Just practice the real thing, orCreate an artificial project or environment.In abstract subjects, the place you want to apply these skills is less obvious.
Gaining a deeper knowledge of a subject will make it more flexible for future Transfer. The more you master, the more you Transfer. (The more languages you know, the easier to learn a new one)
Strategies direct learners use:Project-based learning.Immersive learning. Surround yourself with the target environment in which the skill is used. (Language immersion, joining skill communities)Flight simulator method. What matters for Transfer is the cognitive features. Simulating an environment will work if the simulation matches the environment.Overkill approach. Increase the challenge so that the skill level required is wholly contained within the goal that is set. (Speak at middle-schools instead of toastmasters). Put yourself in an environment where the demands are extremely high so you don't miss important lessons or feedback. This may feel quite intense. These fears are only temporary. If you start, you can often do it longterm. Aim for a particular test, performance, or challenge that will be above the skill level you strictly require. (Publish your work for scrutiny)


Learn straight from the source.Where and how will this knowledge manifest itself? Am I doing anything to tie what I'm learning to that context?If not, this is likely problematic.
Practice isn't enough on it's own.

..................
Drill - attack your weakest point:Like piano - take care of the bars, and the piece will take care of itself.
Your weakest points are like bottlenecks, limiting the speed of your progression.
Drills: simplify a skill enough so that you can focus your cognitive resources on a specific aspect.Drills take apart the direct skill into parts.
Drills vs direct learning.Direct then drill - method:Direct - learn language by speakingAnalyze and isolate componentsDevelop Drills and practice components separatelyIntegrate what you learn in direct practice again.
Earlier in skill: more switching between Drills and direct practiceLater toward mastery: more drilling, as you likely have lots of understanding of the skill and lots of direct practice done or built into schedule.
Designing a drill for improvement:Can be difficult.Timeslicing - isolate a slice in time of the longer sequence in action. Like a bar in a symphony. Layup in a basketball game.Cognitive components - Grammer vs vocabulary.Copycat - when practice of aspects is difficult to do in Isolation. Copy parts of the skill you don't want to practice from someone else, and only drill the parts you do need to practice. (Like getting a movie scene for practicing film scoring)Drawing other drawings. Editing work you have done in the past.Magnifying glass method - spend more time on one component of the skill than you would otherwise. Spend longer on specific components.Prerequisite chaining - start with skill you don't have all the subskills for. Learn as you go. Go back during the process to subskills to learn in greater detail.

Drilling takes work
.................
Retrieval - test to learn:
It is better to wait and recollect than look at the book again.
Learning strategies:ReviewingTestingConcept mapping
Self-testing is what works best.Passive review has no feedback. Concept mapping is similar.
Judgements of learning - jol. If tasks feel like a struggle, we feel we have not learned them. Of they feel easy, we feel we have learned.
Whether you are ready or not, retrieval is helpful.
Free recall > cued recall.Cued recall > multiple choice.Delayed testing > immediate testing
Difficulty is part of the reason retrieval works.
Greater difficulty is more efficient.Things recalled are remembered more deeply when in difficult situations.
Testing is more efficient than review.Retrieval helps you prepare to learn better.Trying to find answers you don't know yet, helps reinforce search strategies.By confronting information you don't know, your mind reorganizes to find solutions.
Nobody has time to master everything.Some things are for mastery, some for recognition/application.
Knowledge that isn't in your head can't be used in direct practice.
Nearly any fact is online, but not having something in your head makes it more difficult to solve hard problems.
Great programmers know lots of ways to solve a problem, and can select the best one.
Tactics:Flashcards: Easy for invariable relationships. One to one relationships.Free recall: after reading or listening, write down as many things as you can remember.Question book method: rephrase ideas as questions to be answered. Don't lazily restate facts as questions. Rephrase the big idea or concept that is implicitly there, requiring thinking. One question per section of text.
Create a list of challenges for laterClosed book learning: try concept mapping without the book..................
Feedback - don't dodge the punches:
Everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth...................
Retention - don't fill a leaky bucket:..................
Intuition - dig deep before building up:...............
Experimentation - explore outside your comfort zone:................

1. Do your research: what topic you will learn, and approximate scope (start narrow). Primary resources you will use. A benchmark for how others have learned this skill. Direct practice activities. Backup materials and drills. 2. Schedule your time. Decide in advance. Stay consistent if you can. Some tasks have long warmup times. Length of time for project. If you are unwilling to out time into your scheduling, you are likely unwilling to do the learning. 3. Execute. In some cases you won’t have the perfect execution. Can you improve it in Meta learning? Focus? Directness? Drill? Retrieval? Feedback? Retention? Intuition and deep understanding? Experimentation? These principles serve as directions not destinations. 4. Review your results. Not all projects are successful. The problems with projects can be often traced back to their inception, not our lack of willpower or ability. Successful projects are also worth analyzing. Hone and advance your learning process. 5. Maintain or master what you've learned. Maintenance (setting up a regular habit, integrate into life), relearning (generally easier than first time learning, subjects you need infrequently), mastery (initial projects offer new projects for subject followup). Not everything one learns needs to be done in a dramatic fashion. Example 1: low-intensity habits. Reading books. Day to day encounters. This works well for accumulation. Ultralearning is best for dealing with frustration barriers and psychological obstacles. Sometimes what is fun isn’t easy, and what’s easy isn’to effective. You can learn and grow to love what you learn, and at some point, your level of skill  makes the subject more fun to learn. Example 2: formal education. Train focu. Lets  Play and work blend seamlessly for children.  Teach people to learn on their own. Ultralearning is intrinsically driven, not extrinsically like formal education. You don’t need to feel that you are good at something to keep learning it, just that you could be good. It’some tempting to identify with labels of good or bad, and to compare ourselves with others. Many ultralearners chose vocations or areas of learning that were unordinary or abnormal, which made it harder for them to compare themselves to others. This is a learning approach, assigning people to projects they don’t know how to solve, just on the cusp of their learning or skill.  The more one learns, rhe more questions come up. Knowledge  increases ignorance, increased learning means both confidence and deep humility.  Our learning projects show us how much further we could have gone.  Our confidence is not arrogance, because we humbly know we have not learned yet, but we know we can learn.  Many things in life have a saturation point, but learning does not. Curiosity has a never ending life, the more we learn, the more we enjoy learning.

Title: Awe
Author: Dasher Keltner
Notes: Awe is a part of the human experience. Awe is not always pleasant, sometimes an experience of dread. Chapter 7 about music is a great explanation of why music is meaningful to humanity, and how it expresses what we cannot express in other ways. How music speaks to us. Also reminded me of How to Hold a Cockroach when it addressed the fact that we don’t know what death is like. Let the dying experience death, don’t paint the picture for them or for ourselves. Be curious.

Title: Cerce
Author: Madeline miller
Notes: Reminded me of the mystery of ancient life, meeting other tribes, nature known and unknown, and the Superstition inherent in ignorance. Also reminded me of Dr. Stone, where science is like sorcery. It is scary to those who don’t understand it, and is different than the inherent power the gods or humanity. It must be learned by experiment, and seems to be governed by other laws. I like the end where she seems to rid herself of her inhibitions and regrets by living out her desires and trying to put things right. The maiden mother matriarch archetype, the triple goddess. She is wildly and naively infatuated, she bares children, and then learns to leave it all. All with a feminist twist of seeing the pain and irrationality of it all, showing bad practical examples rather than good of her experience, offering more of the positive only in her reflection on what has transpired or her acceptance of it or aging.

Title: How to know a person
Author: David Brooks
Notes: Our posture toward the world: what we look for, what we project out onto the world. A physical and mental presence that we bring to others. What is our gaze/expression that we bring to others? We find what we seek in this posture. When we look for beauty, we find wonders. Attention is a moral act, because it creates and brings into being. Active curiosity, a posture of love toward others, is the way to know others. Knowing is a whole body experience (emotion, intellection, touching, thinking). One of our delusions is that any person can be qualified in some way, or classified by some term. Any man manifests certain things at one point and others at another. The same man, but different at different times. Labels are not useful. How does this unique person encounter this other unique person. Morality is about how you pay attention to others. The essential immoral act is the inability to see others. Love is knowledge of the individual. Accompaniment = doing something next to someone. Float down the river with them. Let other people be themselves, open to whatever may come. Be lingerable: the type of person people like to linger with. Willingness, not willfulness. Accompaniment is about presence. You don’t have to say something to someone in a hard time, but you do have to be there. Negative effort: the ability to hold back and let things flow, being lingerable. People need to know that you respect their stuff, that you respect their holding back. Playfulness, people are more human when they play. Each person processes events differently because of what they experience and interpret in their past and present. A person’s whole perspective, how they see the world, can be transformed. We see things as we are, not as the things are. We have only subjective access to an objective reality. Seeing is a process or prediction/projection on what we actually see and perceive. It is extremely flawed. The art of hearing others. Be a loud listener. A good conversation is an exploration. Create a communal effort or collective discovery in the conversation. Treat attention as an on/off switch, be all in. Active listening is an invitation to others to express. Favor familiarity, people like to talk about things they know or are attached to. Make people authors not witnesses, help people really revisit the moment, what their experience was like. Ask specific questions about how the details of what they experienced, and how they experienced it. Don’t fear the pause, take time to reflect before responding, because you can’t listen while you are preparing to respond. A good conversationalist is a midwife. A midwife doesn't give birth, she assists the other in their creation. Sometimes it takes another to help us see our own personal truths. They can help us get distance from problems we are too immersed in to see. Job interviews: Will a person be kind/generous, are they skilled in one thing. Most people don’t escape high school. What were they like in high school, how did they interact with and see others? Kids aren’t afraid of blunt questions. Asking questions can be a vulnerable thing. In a world of security, we ask fewer questions, we assume and don’t venture into discomfort and uncertainty. Perspective receiving, not perspective taking. Worst questions are evaluative (closed questions, questions that imply “i’m about to judge you”). Instead, surrender power, give freedom to go as deep or shallow as possible, open-ended, but not vague and uncaring. People long to be asked questions about who they are. Ask big questions that lift people out of the ruts they are in (why you? Why is that a problem for you? What’s working really well in your life? What do you keep postponing? What would you do if you weren’t afraid? What is the best way to grow old? What crossroads are you at? If you died tonight, what would you regret not doing? If we meet a year from now, what will we be celebrating? If the bext five years is a chapter in your life, what is that chapter about? Can you be yourself where you are and still fit in? What have you said yes to that you no longer believe in? What forgiveness are you withholding? How have you contributed to the problem you are trying to solve? What is the gift you currently hold in exile? What are you most selfconfident about? Have you ever been solitary without being lonely? Which of your five senses is strongest? What has become clearer to you as you’ve aged?). People are a lot more willing to be vulnerable than you think. People long to be asked questions about who they are. People always talk if you listen. Few have ever truly been listened to in their lives. The lonely become bad actors, those unrecognized and unsoothed and unincluded become the few who are “problematic”, we create our “enemies”.  Every conversation operates upon an underlining frame or prerequisite perspective. We should spend less time reverting to our own frames or arguing about frames and more time operating from their frame and seeking to understand it. Those with less power have more awareness of how others see or listen to them. We project our individual mental experiences into the world and thereby mistake our mental perception to be the world. We see affordances. Our power expands our sense of capacity/capability, or field of influence in perception, what we look for. The illuminator model: morality is a social practice, character is not gained alone, people need to be and feel seen by others or be illuminated. What matters in this model is how skillful someone is in interacting with others, in these tasks of illuminating and learning moral interaction/connection with others. We construct/organize our stories about ourselves, only when prompted to do so. By asking others to tell their stories, we help them craft and build their narrative. They find the patterns as we ask them to. People don’t look to their posterity if they don’t look back to their ancestors. The presence of the past, how the dead live in us. How do your ancestors show up in your life? Those with wisdom are like coaches, who really see you, and help you process your emotions and experiences. They prod you along until you understand for yourself. They create an atmosphere of sharing, exchange, seeing, compassion. Wisdom is about reflection and connection with others. Friends hold up a mirror, helping us discover ourselves. Wisdom is a social practice, a community of truth. If equal affection cannot be, let the more loving one be me. Attention is a moral act. It brings things into being. Evil happens when people are unseen, when we fail to see the humanity in others. Truly seeing others is one way we live virtuously, and paying them the right kind of attention is how we truly love.

Title: Greater than the sum of our parts
Author: Richard c schwartz
Notes: C’s of self: curiosity, calm, confidence, compassion, creativity, clarity, courage, and connectedness. Self-leadership. “Self” is in everyone, like the soul, chi, etc. It is the energy of divinity. The ego is a part of cluster of parts. Self is our seat of consciousness. When you are in self, you don’t imagine yourself from the outside. The Buddhist “no self” is the absence of parts, or the true self and inner being. At our core, all of us are this benevolent being, we can identify with it and be happy to know of our goodness. When we see people as one mind, not multiplicity of parts, then it’s easy to shame and judge them, and label them. When we see the multiplicity in everyone, we can have compassion for them and see that parts of them behave destructively, but that is not who they are. Even those who don’t get good parenting or have good role models have this self to access if they work at it. When you are self-lead, you are present, fully embodied, able to care and be with your parts and other people. When your leg aches, you automatically move your arm to soothe it. This is how our parts operate, and how we behave toward others when in self. When self-lead, you feel both the vulnerability of your parts and to your transcendent aspects. Flow state is self. Self-lead people act morally out of an innate sense of connection to other people and their pain. Shamanism has a similar idea of the inner world, a place to go through song, dance, substance, etc. Internal systems, a family systems model within. Restore self-leadership. When a part agrees to not overwhelm you, it will keep to that agreement. There is nothing inside of you that has power over self when you are in self. Self is more powerful. Parts will begin to open up and relax as they realize they are powerless against self. Respectfully ask parts to relax and listen to them a bit if needed. It’s easy to objective people, and it’s easy to objective parts. If you’re in self, parts that come up are not intimidating to you, they are things you can handle. Why we disembody: protectors mistakenly feel they need to protect the self by bringing it out of body, protectors tend to lead you to acgivities that further disembodyand have disregard for the body, being in your body gives you more access to exiles which scares your protectors, protectors generally think you are the age you were when they needed to step up and you were too weak or unskillful  to protect yourself, when you are mebodied it is more difficult for your protectors to do what they feel is necessary and dominate. Body as a sacred temple that holds the soup or spirit. Self heals. Self needs access to the body.  The goal is to show protectors and other parts that you are much more capable, that they don’t need to do what they have done. When you are not in the drivers seat, parts will likely run the machine. They have the ability to numb your body, create habits that cause harm or friction, etc. Many medical symptoms are exacerbated by parts, while most are not caused by them. Your parts speak to you in the way they can, like pain from arthritis. Our medical system unfortunately often kills the messenger, mutes the symptoms rather than listening. We should not strive to be always in self, Buddha led, etc. We are shooting for a kind family approach, the ability to manage your parts, a soft gentle inner parenting style. Be kind and step in when necessary. Drive the bus, but don’t over-manage or legal your way to discipline. No shame, only compassion and strength. Curiosity. Patience, understanding. Open to the messenger, don’t kill it or cut it off. When a water buffalo is stuck in the marsh, it’s the frogs who suffer. We often keep speaking from the water buffalo, and ignore the frogs who suffer. Speaking protector toward each other instead of compassion toward the exiles or other parts. Care for your parts in a nurturing way. Self energy is contagious. A critical mass creates momentum. Self isn’t attached to immediate success. Self has a long view, a longterm goal of flourishing. May the self be with you (lol).

Title: Memoirs of an addicted brain
Author: Marc lewis
Notes: A captivating story, presenting a view of the issues and developmental setbacks that lead to and prolong/encourage addictions, as well as descriptions of the neuroscience/brain changes that occurs in this process. I found it useful to consider the internal dialogue and experiences that the author had, and how that led him to substance abuse and a long-lasting addiction. It all started with not having a safe space when he was young. When he got bullied, he had no home to return to, no loving parents to welcome him when he was not welcome other places.

Title: You’re invited
Author: Jon levy
Notes: Creating trust, ordered by importance: 1) benevolence, 2) honesty/integrity, 3) competence. Halo effect: we are more likely to trust people who our friends or acquaintances trust. The IKEA effect, hazing, and sunk cost fallacy: we place more value on what we have put effort into. Vulnerability precedes trust, by creating vulnerability loops of vulnerability and acknowledgement. You need to find a problem big enough that others' help is needed. It reminded me of family, because having children is a problem where both parents no longer can do it themselves, and the first child is totally new, so they have to rely on each other to make it work and be humble or notice when the other person needs help and do something about it, because otherwise the family effort doesn’t succeed. When intimacy/vulnerability loops are completed, Oxytocin is released. We bond through vulnerability and acceptance of and a helping hand extended toward others’ vulnerability. The IKEA effect is the opposite of impressing or winning people over. Create a problem big enough that requires everyone’s support. At the influencers dinner, this is preparing a meal in less than an hour so that everyone attended can eat. Suddenly everyone is involved, and needed, and since few would be experts, vulnerability loops are frequent. CONNECTING: we connect with people who are most familiar. The most familiar in our life is ourself. So we tend to connect with those who are most similar to ourselves. In dating apps, anything that reminds us of ourselves becomes appealing. The Mere Exposure Effect: being exposed to something causes us to like it more. This is why when you listen to a mediocre song 20 times, it starts to become enjoyable. This is the only reason the world cares about the Mona Lisa. The more people have in common, the more likely they are to connect. We have multiplex relationships. A plex is one commonality. People who we connect with that are different from us often have many more plexs that are common with us. We end up with our friends because they are like us, and they live nearby. We more often connect with people that are closer in distance. Even with desks in an office, the people with closer desks are more likely to connect and communicate. We feel comfortable with what we know, so we often model our parents’ careers, etc.  Belonging includes : membership, influence, integration and fulfillment of needs, shared emotional connection.  Member ship includes boundaries between in and out group members, emotional safety, identification to belong, personal investment or something to do, and a common symbol or such. People need to have influence in the group, some way to participate. If they can’t contribute, then they don’t have influence, and it’should a one-way relationship. (Need to rally around something big enough that everyone’s input and help is needed).  It doesn’t have to be grandiose,  just a give-and-take. Our minds take shortcuts, mental biases. We can design a path to deal with the consequences of these biases, a path to direct the elephant, so the rider does not have to do heavy lifting. Most businesses start with the invitation/ad/pitch/discovery, but that is backwards (start with the end in mind). Membership, engagement, then discovery. What do we want people to feel/think/do? What will lead to this type of membership? What attracts the right people to engage in this way? when we offer from the place of membership and our values, people self-select in or out. We don’t start driving without a place in mind and just hope to end up somewhere nice. Look at the end result (membership) and ask yourself what kind of membership you want to create. How do you want people to interact with you?  In discovery, Create curiosity with information gaps (that are neither too large or too small).  Leave them with a manageable curiosity, raising some questions, but not overwhelming uncertainty or uninteresting ambiguity.  Just be sure that the experience meets expectations and is worth it. Don’t click bait people, or lie, as it will ruin your reputation. If I shared with a participant, someone i’m not friends with, every aspect of the design of the experience, would they feel manipulated or would they appreciate the thoughtfulness?  Always state if you have a brand involved. Protect the community, and don’t agree to bad deals with external organizations like brands, etc. Stay true to your values. If you truly have the participant’s best interest at heart, the messiness of your first events and the flaws in your approach can often be overlooked, and create a vulnerable state for others to join. Growing pains are good if you are benevolent. Trust in your competence can be built if you are honest, and benevolent. Try giving people a way to unwind and some transition time to make starting an engagement or gathering less awkward, by giving them some job to  do or giving a tour. Don’t leave them to their own devices, help them get the ball rolling, make it easy to participate, easy to attend.  Big parties: if you had only 10% the budget, how would you accomplish the same goal? 10% of that? Etc. Until you get to the heart of the matter.  There are always creative solutions that can help build more meaningful connections. The may require more thinking but tend to be less expensive. “How can we accomplish the same business impact with far less logistics and expense?” hiring celebrities can create a need to outdo the last activity, to get someone even bigger. Make sure celebrities are on-brand, and consider making them a surprise, even getting lesser-known talent as a hipster move or mutually beneficial collaboration. Make sure talent is not always the same style, switch it up to avoid needing to top your last event. But again, what does this talent have to do with your brand? Your competitor can likely hire the same talent. Choose wisely, have a purpose, a connection, a reason they represent and facilitate the connection between customers and your brand.

Title: The miracle morning
Author: Hal elrod
Notes: Anitsnooze morning: 1) set an empowering intention before bed, 2) move alarm clock across your room, 3) brush your teeth, 4) rehydrate with water, 5) get into workout clothes. SAVERS. S: silence (prayer, meditation (ifs, mckonkie, embodying helpful emotional states for the day), mindfulness, contemplation), get out of bed and perhaps leave your bedroom. A: affirmations (no lies, active language about what you can do—no passive language), what you are committed to, why it’s important to you, which actions you’ll take and when. Read once a day, recite with emotion. V: visualization (intentional mental rehearsing, imagination, fulfilling certain desires/actions), 1) put yourself in a good mindset, 2) visualize ideal outcome, 3) visualize exactly what you need to do today to progress toward goal. E: exercise. R: read (a good book, self-development, positivity, enoblement). S: scribing (journal your accomplishments, gratitude, learning, progress, goals, joy). You can choose to see the positive, or choose to see the negative. Two pages, two options. Choose gratitude. Some people justify their negativity by saying it’s “realistic”. But what’s realistic is that you have a lot to be grateful for, and you can choose to be grateful, or choose to be in turmoil. Celebrate the good. What we focus on determines how we feel. ABC: accept life exactly as it is, be grateful for each moment, choose your optimal state of consciousness (peace). All inner turmoil is caused by our resisting reality. We naturally wish things were different, and are unaware that this resistance to reality is causing our emotional pain. Things out of our control are not worth pain. Resisting doesn’t change those things, just our increase in pain. Choose acceptance, not resistance. Eating makes you tired, so eat after the miracle morning. Drink water when you wake up to rehydrate.  30 days to form a habit: first q0 days are unbearable, second 10 days are uncomfortable, and third 10 days are unstoppable. After this, you are well-equipped to keep this habit going. In the first ten days, people don’t realize that these first days are temporary, that the unbearableness will go away after you get past a certain number of days. It will not always feel that terrible, it will get easier. Any moment can be the best of our life if we are truly present and grateful. We choose how we interpret life experiences. Living the miracle morning, evening, life, is not just for you, but for others as you bring your best self to them.

Title: Anti-time management
Author: Richie norton
Notes: Life is like a cake. We don’t wait til later to find the sweetness. We put the sugar in at the start and then bake it. We must start living our values now if we want them to be in the end product. Cutting time now to get more later doesn’t work. Time = today is my everything. Prioritize attention. It’s irrational to think that a cake baked without sugar will come out of the oven with sugar in it. We don’t work for money, we work for what we can do with the money. What’s the why of your why? Why do you earn money? Don’t save your dreams, dreams melt like ice cream. The tree is already in the seed. Start with the tree. Making is greater than chasing. The final cause is the seed. Personal purpose: just for you. Professional purpose: for your career, what value to create. People purpose: what people come to mind? What do I need to do for them? People priorities are the most important and difficult to maintain. Play purpose: priorities that fill your soul and energize you. If you could do just one priority from each of these 4 purposes, what would they be? Do those 4 priorities, your priorities of final cause. Focus on these. Put them at the center of your life. Do this as many times as you want. Begin where you are.

Title: I’m glad my mom died
Author: Jennette McCurdy
Notes: Her mom was clearly unwell and seems to have been in denial about her whole life because almost every big choice she made would make it worse. A lot of stuff was going on here, as well. Poverty, hoarding, mental issues, trauma, etc. Her mom was messed up, and she just couldn’t handle living it alone, so she messed up her girl so she could feel her pain was bearable and that her desires were justified. I liked hearing about how she wanted to go to church so badly. That shows how terrible her home life was.

Title: Out of the silent planet
Author: C. S. Lewis
Notes: Interesting planet that the character explores. Lots of beautiful imagery that changes as you read along, and interesting theological ideas. For example, some beings travel fast enough that they are in more than one place at a time, so would it not be possible that a being could travel fast enough or be of the speed fast enough that the are everywhere at once? Those with evil or moral issues are called bent. Bent meaning that something in them has been distorted or twisted, virtue bent into vice. “Bent one”. They learn Bentness from the exiled God (devil). I liked the description of pink or purple weed, the softness and lesser gravity on the planet, the interaction between species.

Title: The practice
Author: Seth godin
Notes:
Art is selfanointing. Anyone is an artist if they say so. Art is a generous offering to others, what we do to make something new to change someone. Leadership, not management. A process or journey, rather than a formula. Creativity is an action, not a feeling. Action will change how we feel. Waiting for a feeling is a luxury we don’t have time for. We inherit stories. We try to make those stories true, because that is more comfortable. If we believe we are not talented enough, we will do whatever we can to make that story true. We sit back and wait to be chosen. The stories we live come from somewhere, and they live in the actions we take. If you want to change your story, change your actions first. We become what we do. Flow is a symptom. We do the work, and flow shows up or not. Flow is not the cause, but the symptom of our work. Better is better than doing more. When you learn trust in yourself, you find passion. Only after we do the work and trust the process does it become our passion. Love what you do, is how we find passion. Choosing creativity is a commitment to a process, not an outcome. We’ve been brainwashed to think that work is about measurable results, that failure is fatal, and we should be sure the recipe is proven before we begin. Embrace a different pattern, a pattern with no guarantees. You can't decide to paint a masterpiece, you just work hard. The world’s worst boss, is in you. We need a boss who raises the bar, but is still merciful. We need a boss who will see us for what we are capable of. We are enough. Already enough. Already see enough , want to make things better, etc. Start where you are, start now, and care enough to do. Decisions: a good decision is separate from what happens next. Decisions are good even if outcomes aren't. What we seek and what we create aren’t the same. Focusing on outcomes at the expense of decisions is a shortcut that will destroy your work. The practice has nothing to do with guarantees. If anyone can do it, then hire anyone. Guarantees are endless pursuits, impossible. Imposter syndrome is a sign you’re healthy. Our work requires us to do things we have never done before. Confidence is a feeling we get when we imagine we have control over the outcome. All athletes have confidence, yet 50% lose. If you require a guarantee, you’ll never start. Engage in the practice with generosity. You're an imposter, but this is proof you’re leading, innovating, creating. You’re an author. The only choice you have is to begin where you are. It is a commitment to the process, the only thing you control. We are easily confused by “I am”. 6 ft tall is a given, but “I am a chef” is a choice. I am of service, is something we each get to choose. It’s not easy to switch from compliance to a new way of being, but the discomfort is a good sign, a sign you're beginning to see the pattern. It’s not the musical skills at 11 years old, it’s the habit of identity. What matters is that you decide on who you are. A practice in service of your identity. Acting as if…is how we acquire identity. Do the work…become the artist. You will find so much more juice if you do it in front of others. It establishes your identity. So far, not yet. You haven’t done such and such, not yet. You haven’t reached your goals, so far. Magic is magic because we don’t know the trick. Our awe disappears when we know the trick. The trick isn’t a trick at all, it’s a practice that we show up and do. Others earn trust by coming through in difficult moments. As we engage in the process, we begin to trust the process. We come to know what to expect from ourselves. The catch is a side effect of the practice. We can’t force a fish to bite, but we can commit to the practice. Every career is a stretch of connected small bridges, each just scary enough to dissuade most people. Bring people discomfort. To create change, we must create discomfort.  Sharing ideas is like sharing the secret to clean water, it’s better for everyone.  Peculiar means specific Or unique. The world needs Peculiar people in a world that suffers from monotony and propagates sameness. Find a way to not hide. Do it again, as many times as it takes to learn to not hide. It’s calming to be reassured, but the feeling never lasts. Certainty isn’t required. Hope is not the same as being reassured. Hope is the confidence in self that you have a shot to take and it may or may not work.  Confidence is not absolute. Choose actions that will generate feelings you want. The practice is a choice.  Embrace “yet”.  The magic is that you choose to share your art. You can do more than you know, if you do it for someone else. Cynicism is a defense mechanism.  Empathy is for those who receive it. Empathy is not for the unbelievers.   You must make work for those who want it, because it can’t cater to everyone. Make work that matters a great deal to someone. Choose to be Peculiar. Choose the journey, commit to the journey, not outcome. The audience isn’t wrong, you’re just not right yet. Shipping work means it’s for someone, someone other than you. You make work for you, and work for others, but both at the same time is not appropriate, or likely doable. 
The enrolled are committed to the journey. .those who hate the art signed up for something else. It’s not for them.  Selfish is a choice. To the drowning man, everyone is a stepping stone.  Attachment is a choice. Do we attach to outcomes, other’s perceptions, etc.? The good news is that there is nothing to hold onto. Let go and go back to the practice. Becoming unattached gives us a foundation.  How often do you offer a competitor?  A mindset of abundance. Not everything we offer is for everyone. Offering alternatives is a sign of generosity, not grasping. Offer competitive. No one owes us anything, and it is in our interest to act as if they don’t. Do work simply because we can. The feeling of being owed destroys honest work. The feeling of being owed is toxic.  Asking “why” forces you to truly look at something. That’s brave and generous, rather than avoidant. If you knew you were sure to fail, what would you do? If you fail, would it be worth it to pursue the journey? Separate the process from the outcome.  It’s selfish to hold back any idea iwitheld is an idea taken away. You are the lifeguard. It’s your job to share. Worrying isn’t productive because it doesn’t produce confidence.  To cater to the masses means to he average, because the masses mean average.  Better clients demand more, they have better taste. You earn better clients by doing the work that better clients want, not hype doing better work for bad clients. Who are you doing the work for? It’s only for them. You don’t paint your house for someone across the country. Who can you reach? We do what we can, and others do the same. If we bring others along, we accomplish more. We have the ability to create change for our audience, the person  we accept as our client, not to do work beyond criticism.  You should only care about those who are willing to engage. The believers are tired of being ignored, and are eager to be brought on board.  We then make for others, understanding what they want. If we don’t want to make what they want, we make for someone else. What is it for?  Successful people get good at filtering what appears in their consciousness. They reject ideas that “won’t work”. Mindfulness is healthy, professional, and difficult, especialy in a culture that values busyness, not intentionality. We don't reject busyness, but we should value intention. Authenticity is a trap. We always calculate, we make intentional acts. We idealized authenticity. If we have any self-control, we are not being authentic. Your audience wants your consistent voice, not authentic voice.  Reaper than real: crafted, invent something, be consistent, make crafted art, inauthentic.  It’s difficult to be consistent, deliberate, etc. It’s generous, you choose to do it, rather than being authentic or based on whim. . Credentials have expanded to keep people out who would make change. High achievers are taught to sacrifice independent thought for a good grade. Credentialing doesn’t have the power it does if we didn’t accept our uncredentialed status. What about fake experts? Credentials are what create fake experts. Those with credentials can hide behind them.  It’s OK to maintain the status quo. A chef may be successful because they keep to what most people expect when they go out for dinner. Writer’s block, is a myth.  We invented writer’s block. It is a story, but it can change. The search for certainty is  at the heart of our block. To be creative is to be at the frontier. Polish is overrated. Perfectionism is too much shine, polish, manufacturing. Failure is the foundation of our work. The only way to find something new is the willingness to be wrong on ourbway to be right. The process requires originality, and intention. Creative leaders fail. All of us have a narrative. Our story us about how the world works.  It informs our choices, and our ability to make change in our culture. Is the narrative working? If it’so getting in your way, it probably needs to change.  It’s hard to get blocked when you are moving, even if it’s in a direction you didn’t expect. The process is infinite if we let it be. Play to keep playing. The infinite game has no winners or lovers. A marathon is an infinite game. It’s largely about about cooperation, not direct competition. What we don’t see is others’ years of long lonely runs. If you run a marathon, you get tired. Everyone gets tired, fear, etc. Where do you put the tired, fear, etc.? Yes, and…? Never no. Yes, this happened,  and …? The lesson of improv is the power of absurdity. And uncertainty. We let the ego subside and acknowledge the fear. Understanding the process can make you funny regardless of who you are. We become creative because we ship work. Anchors can drag us down, but can also be a beacon, drawing us to outcomes we promised. Criticism reminds us of the outcomes, not the process. Most critics are unskilled and ungenerous. A generous critic is priceless, and they are ready to be enrolled in your journey. Say thank you to these critics. They tell you what would work for them. Some critics tell us a lot about them, and thus help us know it is not for them. We can say, “it’s not for you”. True fans require idosyncracy. If all they wanted was the top 40, they wouldn’t find it from you.  If the practice you developed isn’t paying, you can thank it and move on. Sunk costs and defensiveness.  Sunk costs must be ignored. There are at least 45 ways we sacrifice our work to our fear: (Expand work so we don’t finish. Stall.  Shrink project so it doesn’t matter. Ship crap. Ship perfect work. Refuse to listen to generous critics. Listen to well-meaning but chicken critics.  Sacrifice work for commercial shortterm. Hide from deadlines. Become a diva. Compromise on good parts. Compromise hard parts. Assume inspiration lies in drugs. Don’t go to work. Work all the time. Wait for the muse. Talk about the work too early, looking for reason to abandon it. Don’t talk with right people about the work, crippling it.  Define the work as you and you as the work. Work only when inspiration strikes. Fall behind on domain knowledge. Copy everything. Copy nothing. Embrace jealousy. Taunt yourself. Announce that important work takes longer. Expect applause. Demand cash  commensurate with effort or insight and hold back until it arrives. Avoid sales calls. Read your reviews. Memorize your reviews. Respond to your reviews. Catastrophic. Focus on impending or eventual death. Assume immortality as a way of stalling. Listen to people who are afraid. Confuse perfectionism with quality. Hold on tighter as ship date approaches. Let go too soon as ship date approaches. Miss ship dates regularly. Don’t set ship dates. Redefine your zone of contribution to be smaller than it needs to be, letting yourself off the hook. Surround yourself with people who Hage small dreams. Polish your excuses. Pretend you Have writer’s block.) The option of vulnerability.  Learning is a choice. You are not your work. You can always learn. We feel like it because we write. Write to clarify, write to challenge yourself. Writing puts you on the hook. Poetry is not like reasoning. There is an abundance of poems, infinite poems to write. The bogeyman is not real. Denying is existence. Creators flee the bogeyman everyday. As soon as you look him in the eye, he vanishes.  Seeing the tools and ingredients ready and prepared with care opens the door for intentional action. The internet and such brings uninvited energy, because it has infinite ideas and distractions. It’s tempting to give credit to the muse for our genius.  Flow is a result of effort. Set up your tools , turn off the internet, and go back to work. Desirable difficulty: random difficulties, less enjoyable, but they set us up for success in the long run. Sign up for days , weeks, years of desirable difficulty.batting practice is a practice. Nike's slogan error is not helpful advice. Don’t just do it, merely do it. Focus on process, not outcome. Yes and. Ignore what you cannot control. You need more bad ideas.  There was a bad idea, and then there was a better idea.   The wild side. “How do I make this better” is different than “how do I make this”. Get a pencil. This is scarce. Most people won’t draw up plans. Creation isn’t fatal. Anchor up. Promises show we believe we have a shot to keep that promise. We promise to ship, we don’t promise the result. What does good mean? It’s a trap, because we might judge good work by commercial success. There is a huge gap between good and as good as it could be, but you will never bridge that gap. No one us keeping you from shipping your work. Do the steps.  Corrolary of self doubt. Most of the feedback we recieve is rejection. The group of people who believe they can also do the work is very large, everyone “is an expert’. The most commercially successful creators simply have the benefit of the doubt plus tribal cognitive dissonance. The world is too busy to receive your truly individual work. Transformation begins with genre. “This is a chocolate bar”, vs “this is a handmade chocolate bar”. You get leverage by beginning with genre. What will I tell my friends, how is it different? We begin with what's the same.  If you choose a genre, you’ve made a series of promises. You only need the smallest breakthrough. Most things are the same. I’ve never met someone who never had a good idea in their head. It’s not that they are better., it’s that they shipped work, and others didn’didn’. Meetings might help, but they probably won’t. Ego assertion, not ego mania. Assertions are not answers, and are  generous. “Perhaps” begins each assertion. Assertions don’don’require authority, they are suggestions and invite others to join the journey. If others don't ’ respond, then they are not enrolled. Swimming is like creativity. No one knows how to swim at first, we all learn. There are no barriers, qualifications, etc. Everyone learns swimming by the process, practice, trying and learning.  None of us are superman, none of us do it all.  Choose a superpower, commit to something. Choose the skill you will assert to the outside world. The goal is to be the best in the world at being you, someone others will choose, even if not everyone. We can teach bravery, creativity, and learning, and we can unteach these things. People eat what they eat because of cultural expectations, etc. Are you aware of what is required on your reading list for your profession? It’s a profession because you know others’ work. The posture of understanding pioneers and current state of industry is true earned skill and profession.  In and of itself: the peculiarity is consistent specific. It shows the fingerprints and idosyncracy of the creator. Constraint: necessary. It’s tempting to despise constraints.  All creativity has constraints. Choose your constraints. Think at the edge of the box, not outside of it.  Change the world, doesn't mean change everything.  Hubris is the dream killer.  You are not the boss, but you are in charge. You are in charge of the change you make in the world.  If you have to ask “should I keep going?” In your exploration, the answer is yes. Life is on the wire, the rest is just waiting. Where is our fuel? Curiosity, generosity, and connection. Human connection is exponential.

Title: The problem of pain
Author: C. S. Lewis
Notes: We regard God as a parachute, and pain forces our attention. Happiness is not enough to make us blessed. God stoops to humility in allowing us pain for our good, for us to have humility and choose Good or God. Death into life. Surrender to God. Pain hurts. Suffering is not good in itself, but in it we can direct ourselves to God. God can make good out of evil. You will serve God however you choose, as Judas or John. It makes a difference to you, but not to God, he makes good of whatever happens. Fasting is different from Missing dinner by accident is different or poverty. Self torture is different from tribulation. Only God can mortify. If tribulation is necessary for redemption, then it will not cease til redemption is finished. We seek security to find comfort in this world, God helps us find insecurity in mortality. Repentance requires correcting the error, and the temptation. But pain requires no such undoing. Suffering only produces pity.

Title: Something missing
Author: Matthew dicks
Notes: I found it funny that he made a mental note to burn his pants when he got home. Funny, clever, and playfully suspenseful. The story is also a story of the character telling his own story, in a way. I liked that the book ended with “he wondered where he would begin”, it makes you want to read it again, because it is his story. It also ends right where he is in the story, anticipating what’s next but not being able to predict it, walking straight into his anxiety and owning whatever happens.

Title: How will you measure your life
Author: Clayton m christensen
Notes:
Theories help us know how to think about things we have not done yet. We can learn without experiencing the pain of every failure. Great lives are a byproduct of happiness and meaning. We don’t find satisfaction and meaning from getting a “good life”. What brings money, does not bring happiness. Hygiene factors (money, status, compensation, job security, etc.) are a byproduct of being happy with your job. Emergent vs deliberate strategy. When you find out what really works for you, then you use a deliberate strategy. Until then, use an emergent strategy, a strategy that emerges as you go along. A modified strategy coalescing from a myriad of day-to-day decisions, to pursue unanticipated opportunities, solving unanticipated problems. Unpredictable results bring unpredictable strategies. How can you decide what has the best choice of working for you? How to decide if you should go with a deliberate strategy or an emergent one, if you should make a big investment of time, etc.? Acknowledge your predictions are rough and inaccurate. Compile a list of assumptions made in these predictions. Rank order the list. Assess which assumptions must be true in order to expect these predictions to become true. Test the validity of the most important assumptions. What assumptions must prove true? Are these assumptions within your control? Are they based on extrinsic or extrinsic motivators? While you are still figuring it out, keep the aperture of your life open.  Continue to experiment until you do find an approach that works.  Expecting to have a clear vision just wastes time and may close off your mind to unexpected opportunities. Change is uncomfortable, being open and experimenting is uncomfortable. Watch where your resources flow.  Where you spend your resources is what you are executing, whether you planned a strategy or not.  Compensation sometimes incentivises expending resources in the wrong areas. Resource allocation is where the rubber meets the road. Vision, plans, and opportunities are all just that until resources are allocated, and they all vy for attention. Look at what you do, not what you say you will do. Pull out the check stub, or account purchase history. High achieving people often direct resources to the activities that yield the most tangible immediate accomplishments/consequences.  Short-term rewards take their resources. Many ambitious people allocate fewer and fewer resources to the things that they say matter most. With every decision about how you allocate your time and money , you are making a statement about what really matters to you. Does your family come out on top? We are tempted to invest energy un whatever activity yields immediate evidence that we have achieved something.  Set boundaries in your life, to keep yourself true to what you most value. The longterm payoff will be much more profound.  The time to invest in meaningful relationships is when it seems it is not necessary.  
Most businesses have to pivot, and yhe successful companies have enough leftover capital to invest in the new strategy after failing. Once a viable strategy has been found, pivot forward.  When we neglect our values, we end up seeking returns later on investments we didn’t make.  Investments in life cannot be sequenced.  By the time we move on to another investment, the game is already over. You have to “spin all the plates”. Face to face conversation and being naturally chatty with a child is important for children. It has a profound effect on children, most importantly in the first year of life . The effect is exponential. Children who have been exposed to extra talk have incalculable advantage. A tiny investment has a huge return. You can’t miss this window. The investment is made long before it seems to pay off. Invest long before you need the fruit.  What job did you hire that milkshake for?  We hire or buy products to do jobs for us. Students hire school to feel accomplished and have something to do. Schools often do a different job, instead of offering students success everyday. Many unhappy marriages are built on “selflessness”  based upon what we want. We give what we think others need. We project what we want, and forget to ask what people really need, what jobs they truly need done. Don’t make a chocolatier milkshake, do the job to be done. The path to happiness is about finding someone who you want to make happy.   We feel attached to things because we have given so much of ourselves to them. Sacrifice deepens our commitment. It’s important that what we sacrifice for is worthy of that commitment.  Thinking of what jobs need to be done allows you to develop true empathy. Then do the job. Don’t outsource the future.  Figure out what capabilities you’ll need to succeed in the future, and keep those in-house.  As parents, we can help our children develop capabilities. They have resources, processes, and priorities. Resources = what you use, processes = how you do it, priorities = why you do it. Many parents are removing the resources by which kids develop processes. They are creating the Greek tragedy of Dell, outsourcing their capabilities and unintentionally inhibiting their children’s growth and development of processes.  Providing opportunities for our kids should serve to solve their jobs, not ours. Don’t outsource your children’s resources and activities without being sure they are productive and that your kids have learned to learn, to think, develop new knowledge, processes, etc. Start early to help children solve problems on their own. Help them build confidence in their capabilities, that they can solve their own problems. They will feel pride that they have done it. Children learn when they are ready to learn. When we outsource, we often outsource our values. They learn when they are ready to learn, and not when we are ready to teach.   If your children get their values and beliefs and priorities from other people, who's children are they? Have you truly patented them? Don’t outsource your role as a parent. If you’re not with your children in their challenges, you are missing an opportunity to shape their priorities and lives. What lessons are you letting your kids have? Those with inadequate experience have taken the wrong courses. Often, enforcing the rules is harder on parents than children.  Help children see success in things you want to be part of your culture.  Your solution to problems will become expected. How you react to events comes to become boreal for your children. They will see what you do as expected, it will become your family culture. If you don’t consciously form culture, it will form, perhaps in a way you don't like. If you  let your children get away with lazy or disrespectful culture a few times will allow it to become culture. So will telling them you are proud of them when they accomplish something.
